title: Hedge Ratio Estimation and Risk–Return Dissociation in Pairs Trading: Kalman Filtering under Structural Instability

authors.name: Pooja Venugopal Baskaran
affiliations: Jarvis College of Computing and Digital Media, DePaul University (Alumni)

abstract: When two equities share a long-run co-movement relationship, the ratio of their price sensitivities (the hedge ratio) determines the directional exposure of a pairs trading position. In practice hedge ratios drift as macroeconomic regimes shift, rendering static estimates stale. This paper characterises how the mode of hedge ratio estimation shapes the risk–return profile of pairs trading strategies, rather than asking whether pairs trading is profitable in aggregate. Two hypotheses are tested with econometric discipline: does Kalman-filtered dynamic estimation statistically reduce tail-risk relative to static OLS (H1), and does a two-state Hidden Markov Model (HMM) regime filter further reduce drawdown (H2)? We evaluate seven estimation branches on 50 S&P 500 equities across the structurally demanding 2020–2024 window, which compresses four macroeconomic regimes (COVID-19 shock, quantitative easing recovery, Federal Reserve rate-hike cycle, and AI-driven sector concentration) into five calendar years. This window is an intentionally selected high-instability evaluation period; results should be interpreted as conditional on this environment and may not generalise to calmer or longer samples. A walk-forward cross-validation design with 14 rolling out-of-sample folds prevents in-sample overfitting; BCa bootstrap confidence intervals on the annualised Sharpe ratio and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on fold-level differences provide formal inference. In this demanding environment, all seven branches produce negative net-of-cost fold-mean Sharpe ratios, confirming that 28-bps round-trip transaction costs consume gross alpha at the 2.3-day average holding periods generated by the Kalman branches. Static OLS achieves a fold-mean Sharpe of −0.157 versus −2.080 for Kalman (OLS dominant in 12 of 14 folds), driven by the Kalman filter’s 54% higher trade turnover (932 vs. 607 pooled trades) that amplifies cost drag. Despite lower net Sharpe, Kalman reduces fold-mean maximum drawdown by 71% relative to OLS (−0.31% vs. −1.07%), a dissociation of return from risk that is the paper’s central empirical finding. For H2, HMM conditioning further reduces fold-mean MaxDD by 30% (to −0.22%, Wilcoxon p < 0.001) while cutting trade frequency by 45%. A mechanism decomposition (Branch D) shows Kalman’s drawdown advantage is consistent with a structural explanation: short holding periods alone do not replicate it; a posterior variance entry gate (Branch F) partially repairs signal quality (52.7%→54.8% win rate) and improves fold-mean Sharpe to −1.38. The estimated Kalman–OLS cost breakeven is 6–7 bps one-way, suggesting that Kalman may be competitive at direct-market-access execution costs while retaining its drawdown advantage.
